author: ohtadmin
title: Cost to battle blizzard nearly $38K
text:
A postmortem from the historic blizzard of ’26 includes a dump truck, generator and $37,500 among the collateral damage from 29 inches of snow.
Town Administrator Ed Mello said the cost for overtime for plow drivers and police officers was $24,000. Materials, including sand and salt, cost $4,000. The remaining $9,500 was used to hire a contractor, M.T. Lott, to plow during the height of the storm. That outlay included labor and equipment.
The line item in the 2025-26 budget to support snow-related events was $88,000. Prior to the blizzard, the town already had spent $48,800 on snow removal expenses this winter.
The oldest vehicle in the fleet, a 2006 Sterling Acterra six-wheel dump truck with 109,000 miles, was disabled while plowing during the snowstorm, which virtually paralyzed the community from Feb. 22-23. Voters, however, already have approved money to replace that truck through a $950,000 bond.
“That truck was on its way out,” Mello said. “We didn’t have any major equipment failures.”
Mello said he expects to recoup some money from that truck, which was towed back to the highway garage due to a damaged drivetrain.
“We’ll advertise that vehicle,” he said. “We sell everything that goes to surplus. We’re pretty successful selling that equipment, too.”
The director of public works, Mike Gray, said the generator at the water treatment plant failed.
“When we anticipate a storm like the blizzard, we will put the generator online,” he said. “There’s a reason for that. There’s a lot of electronic components to our water treatment facility and it doesn’t like power to come on and off, on and off. In advance of a storm, we’ll take the plant off the street power and put it on a generator power.”
Gray immediately called the vendor that services the 18-year-old piece of equipment and was given the bad news upon the company’s arrival.
“We thought it was a simple issue,” he said. “It ended up being a failure of the stator in the generator, which is beyond repair. So basically, that generator is toast.”
Gray said the department currently is renting a generator while he receives quotes for a replacement, which he said should last 20-25 years. Gray said he was surprised the failed generator did not survive the storm.
“There’s not that many hours on it,” he said. “It’s just unfortunate that it happened. We’re trying to figure it out. … I don’t know if it was bringing moisture into the generator because it was very windy that day. I don’t know if some of the windings were exposed. Something happened inside that generator during the storm.”
Gray said Mello is working with the insurance carrier to determine whether the department could recoup any money for the generator.
Mello, who has prepared an initial assessment of the damage for the Federal Emergency Management Agency and Rhode Island Department of Emergency Management Agency, said he also has received claims for a “handful of mailboxes” that were damaged. He said these mailboxes need to have been damaged by the plow itself, not the snow pushed into them, to quality for support. The preexisting condition of the mailbox also “plays a significant factor” in this process, he added.
